To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relative proportion of infiltrating T lymphocytes was similar in Graves' disease (GD) and Hashimoto's Thyroiditis (HT), but that the density of infiltrating T cells was higher in HT than in GD.
the relative proportions of T cell subsets infiltrating into the thyroid in Hashimoto's and Graves' disease are similar, whereas the density of lymphocytic infiltration was much higher in the former.
the thyroid infiltrates in Hashimoto's disease and Graves' disease are predominantly T cells, with more T8 than T4 cells.

immunohistological phenotypes of infiltrating lymphocytes and their distribution in thyroid tissues.
the immunological aspects of Graves' disease and autoimmune thyroiditis.
the immunological mechanisms of autoimmune thyroid disease, especially Hashimoto's thyroidis and Graves' disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immunological abnormalities in the thyroid gland are not specific for either Hashimoto's thyroid disease or Graves' disease.

the thyroid infiltrate in Hashimoto's and Graves' disease consists of a mixture of T and B lymphocytes, the T cells being mainly suppressor/cytotoxic and inducer/helper cells, and the B cells being mainly mature B cells, which may have been stimulated by the T cells to differentiate into immunoglobulin producing cells.
the thyroid infiltrating lymphoid cells in both Hashimoto's thyroiditits and Graves' disease were predominantly T cells, with more T8 than Leu 5 cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Hashimoto's thyroiditisis a T cell mediated autoimmune disease in which B cells are activated to produce autoantibodies.

Hashimoto's thyroidis is characterized by the presence of a high density of activated T cells and a low density of IgD+ B cells in the thyroid interstitium, whereas Graves' disease has a low density of activated T and B cells in the same region.
in autoimmune thyroiditis, the thyroid infiltrating lymphocytic cells are predominantly T3+ T cells with more suppressor/cytotoxic than helper T cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

Hashimoto's thyroid disease and Graves' disease are two distinct diseases, and the differences are not only in the presence of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, but also in the immunological profile of infiltrating T lymphocytes.
there are no major differences in the distribution of lymphocyte subsets in the thyroid of Graves' disease patients versus patients with Hashimoto's thyroidis.
the thyroid gland is a site for the generation of autoreactive T and B cells in both Hashimoto's thyroidis and Graves' disease, and that the thyroid gland may be a target of autoimmune attack.
